extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (PTO), patent attorneys, and attorneys facing OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for determining whether an attorney engaged in unauthorized practice of law before the PTO or federal courts and whether disciplinary rules (PTO and local court rules) were violated. Focuses on pro hac vice requirements, what constitutes practice of law, evidence and credibility standards, and related ethical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on practicing in violation of other jurisdictions (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A] practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction, or assist another in doing so." (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to conduct such as drafting and filing pleadings or advising clients while an attorney's license is suspended in the admitting state; includes assisting others to do so. The Tribunal found drafting/responding to PTO or court filings while suspended constitutes practice in violation of § 11.505.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central District of Illinois pro hac vice/local admission requirements (CDIL-LR 83.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any attorney licensed in any state or D.C. must be admitted to practice generally in this court on written motion of a member in good standing or upon the attorney's own motion accompanied by certification of good standing from the state in which the attorney is licensed. The court does not permit pro hac vice admissions generally; at judge's discretion an attorney may seek leave to participate while application for admission is pending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorneys may not appear, file, or practice before the court without being admitted; persons who exercise privileges before admission or during suspension may be adjudged guilty of contempt. Failure to obtain pro hac vice or general admission means filings or appearances constitute unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: District of Massachusetts pro hac vice/local admission requirements (LR 83.5.3(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney seeking to appear and practice by leave in the District of Massachusetts must file a certificate that (1) he is a member in good standing in every jurisdiction where admitted, (2) there are no disciplinary proceedings pending against him, and (3) he is familiar with the Local Rules; his application must be on motion of a member of the bar of the court who shall file an appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until the application is granted, the attorney may not enter an appearance or sign any papers, except that the attorney may sign a complaint or paper necessary to prevent default only if that paper is accompanied by his application for admission in proper form. Failing to follow these procedural requirements renders appearances and filings unauthorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a complaint or signing pleadings constitutes an appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The filing of the complaint shall constitute an appearance by the attorney who signs it." (LR 83.5.2(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an attorney signs a complaint, the court treats that as the attorney entering an appearance — with attendant obligations and admission requirements. Signing a complaint while not admitted or while suspended is treated as unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local rule on pro se designation and signature
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who appears pro se shall so state in the initial pleading or other paper filed by him; the words 'pro se' shall follow his signature on all papers subsequently filed by him in the same case. (LR 83.5.2(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assisting an unrepresented litigant, an attorney must not sign filings in a way that disguises representation; failing to use the 'pro se' designation properly or signing another's filings can indicate unauthorized representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of practicing law (Massachusetts standard, In re Hrones)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Directing and managing the enforcement of legal claims and the establishment of the legal rights of others, where it is necessary to form and to act upon opinions as to what those rights are and as to the legal methods which must be adopted to enforce them, the practice of giving or furnishing legal advice as to such rights and methods and the practice, as an occupation, of drafting documents by which such rights are created, modified, surrendered or secured."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crafting and prosecuting a sophisticated civil rights lawsuit — drafting complex complaints and directing litigation strategy — falls squarely within the practice of law under this definition. The Tribunal used this to conclude that drafting and managing multi-count complaints constituted practice in Massachusetts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of a form is not dispositive of practicing law (Downtown Disposal Servs. precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney practiced law when he 'merely filled in blanks on a simple form that did not require the use of any legal expertise' — it is not the simplicity of the form but the fact that an appeal or legal right was pursued that matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that preparing a simple notice of appeal did not require legal judgment will not necessarily excuse unauthorized practice; courts look to whether the filing affected a party's rights and required legal judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard for finding misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct was proven by a 'clear and convincing' standard of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Tribunal expressly finds clear and convincing evidence that the respondent engaged in unauthorized practice when factual admissions and documentary evidence demonstrate drafting, filing, and advising while suspended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility expectations when claiming client notification of suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney claiming to have notified a client of suspension should have corroborating evidence; 'Any nominally cautious and competent attorney would notify his client of his suspension in writing or at least create a written memorandum of the notice given for his own record purposes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uncorroborated after-the-fact assertions that a client was verbally notified of suspension are treated as self-serving and may be disbelieved by the Tribunal absent supporting documentation or testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of ghostwriting as a defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Ghostwriting debates assume the ghostwriting lawyer is licensed in the jurisdiction; disclosure that an attorney ghostwrote documents can be tantamount to admitting unauthorized practice where the lawyer is not licensed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article arguments that ghostwriting 'circumvents' signature rules do not excuse conduct when the ghostwriter is not licensed in the jurisdiction; ghostwriting is ethically permissible only where the attorney is otherwise authorized to practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on practicing while suspended is not mitigated by later admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent's unlawful practice is not mitigated by any subsequent pro hac vice admission or later admission to practice in the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct while suspended remains a violation even if at a later date an attorney obtains admission to the court; prior unauthorized practice is not cured retroactively by later admission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5.5(c)(2) (Mass. R. Prof'l Conduct) does not override local federal court admission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 5.5(c)(2) permits temporary legal services under certain circumstances, but compliance with Rule 5.5 does not necessarily equal compliance with the minimal requirements put in place by a federal district court to appear and practice before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a state professional conduct rule contemplates temporary practice, a federal district court's local rules (e.g., mandatory certification, sponsor, and grant of leave) control admission to practice in that court; an attorney cannot rely solely on a state rule to bypass court-specific admission procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements about admission status (e.g., 'pending admission pro hac vice') violate professional conduct rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating that one is 'pending admission pro hac vice' when such a statement is false can violate rules such as 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a), 10.77(b), 10.84(a) and 10.23(b)(4),(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresentations about admission status in filings and not taking required steps for pro hac vice admission constitute separate bases for disciplinary charges in addition to unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective prosecution defense requires proof of both discriminatory effect and discriminatory intent
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed on selective prosecution, a defendant must show 'that the federal prosecutorial policy had both a discriminatory effect and a discriminatory intent.' (citing United States v. Darwich)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalized claims, internet postings, or conspiracy theories do not satisfy the burden; the tribunal rejected selective prosecution claims absent clear evidence of both effect and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice before a U.S. tribunal occurs irrespective of practitioner's physical location
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a practitioner is physically outside the country, his practice can still take place 'before the United States PTO' or other U.S. tribunals and thus be subject to U.S. ethics rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Residency outside the U.S. does not immunize a practitioner from PTO or court disciplinary rules when the relevant acts are done before U.S. tribunals; claiming Canadian residency does not negate the obligation to comply with PTO ethics rules.
